steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Draft the introduction for our paper on fine-tuning large language models without losing their in-context learning ability on unseen tasks. Explain the over-specialization problem, our finding about format specialization, the two-stage prompt-tuning-then-model-tuning method, and list our contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
## Introduction

- LLMs + in-context learning: why they are useful
- Where LLMs still fall short
- Fine-tuning helps but causes over-specialization
- Our finding: format specialization
- Our method: ProMoT (two-stage fine-tuning)
- Experimental highlights
- Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
## Introduction

- LLMs and in-context learning
  - NLP revolutionized by scaling transformer LLMs + large-scale pretraining
  - better downstream performance; can do unforeseen tasks given a prompt
  - in-context learning: re-purpose for specific tasks with minimal supervised data -> fast prototyping/experimentation, esp. low data regime
- Where LLMs lag
  - grounding / eliminating hallucinations; reasoning and logical clarity; mathematics
  - behind best human performance, or fine-tuned performance of same model
- Fine-tuning and over-specialization
  - common practice: fine-tune on one or several specialized tasks
  - causes over-specialization; harms generalization to unseen tasks via in-context learning
  - mT5 fine-tuned on a single task loses few-shot performance on unseen tasks within one thousand steps (shown later)
  - want single model good on supervised fine-tuned tasks and on unseen tasks (hundreds of downstream / unknown tasks)
  - need fine-tuning techniques that prevent over-specialization
- Format specialization
  - loss of in-context learning largely caused by format specialization = overfitting to task format
  - e.g. mT5 fine-tuned on binary classification -> output space only "True"/"False"; can't generate other output styles per prompt
  - happens at very beginning of fine-tuning, before semantic content is learned
- ProMoT (PROmpt Tuning with MOdel Tuning)
  - off-load format learning to small task-specific parameters external to model
  - stage 1: freeze pretrained model, tune small set of extra params (soft prompt before input works well)
  - stage 2: freeze extra params, tune main model
  - format learned first -> mostly goes into extra params
  - inference: remove extra params or not depending on whether task shares the format
- Results
  - significantly alleviates specialization, boosts generalization on semantically related tasks with different formats
  - mT5 XXL fine-tuned only on NLI binary classification -> better in-context summarization than pretrained model (maybe grounding from NLI); Table 1
  - better supervised performance than pretrained + better in-context performance than standard fine-tuning
- Contributions (4)
  - in-context learning decreases in single-task fine-tuning for T5; format specialization as cause, mostly at beginning
  - ProMoT 2-stage framework
  - 10+ NLP tasks: reduced specialization, similar supervised performance; generalization across dissimilar tasks sharing semantics
  - combinable with other (parameter-efficient) fine-tuning; examples with multi-task and 1-shot prompts

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
## Introduction

Natural language processing (NLP) has recently been revolutionized by scaling up large language models (LLMs) based on transformers together with large-scale pretraining. Besides better downstream performance, these pretrained LLMs can also do a broad array of unforeseen tasks when they are given a prompt. This in-context learning capability lets users re-purpose LLMs flexibly for specific tasks with a minimum amount of supervised data, which is very convenient for fast prototyping and experimentation, especially in the low data regime.

But even the largest and most advanced LLMs still have a lot to improve. Grounding and eliminating hallucinations, reasoning and logical clarity, and mathematics are just some examples where LLMs are still behind the best human performance, or in some cases behind the fine-tuned performance of the same model.

The most common way to improve a pretrained model is to fine-tune it on a specialized task or on several tasks. But fine-tuning an LLM usually makes it over-specialized to the fine-tuning tasks, and this harms the generalization ability the model already had on unseen tasks via in-context learning. As we show later, an mT5 model fine-tuned on a single task loses its few-shot performance on unseen tasks within one thousand steps of fine-tuning. When there are hundreds of downstream tasks and even unknown tasks, we want a single fine-tuned model that is good both on the supervised fine-tuned tasks and on general unseen tasks. So it is very important to develop new fine-tuning techniques that prevent these fine-tuned models from over-specializing to only a few tasks.

In this work, we find that the loss of general in-context learning abilities during fine-tuning is to a large extent caused by format specialization, which makes the model overfit to the specific format of the task. For example, if we fine-tune an mT5 model on a binary classification dataset, it learns an output space with only "True" and "False", and it loses its ability to flexibly generate different output styles according to the in-context prompts of other tasks. We show that format specialization tends to happen at the very beginning of fine-tuning, before the model has fully learned the semantic content of the task.

- ProMoT (PROmpt Tuning with MOdel Tuning)
  - off-load format learning to small task-specific params external to model
  - stage 1: freeze model, tune extra params (soft prompt before input)
  - stage 2: freeze extra params, tune main model
  - format learned first -> goes into extra params; at inference keep or drop them depending on task format
- Results
  - alleviates specialization; boosts generalization on semantically related tasks with different formats
  - mT5 XXL fine-tuned only on NLI binary classification -> better in-context summarization than pretrained (grounding?); Table 1
  - better supervised than pretrained, better in-context than standard fine-tuning
- Contributions (4)
  - in-context learning drops in single-task fine-tuning for T5; format specialization, early in fine-tuning
  - ProMoT 2-stage framework
  - 10+ NLP tasks: less specialization, similar supervised performance; generalization across dissimilar tasks
  - combinable with other fine-tuning methods; multi-task and 1-shot prompt examples

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
## Introduction

Natural language processing (NLP) has recently been revolutionized by scaling up large language models (LLMs) based on transformers together with large-scale pretraining. Besides better downstream performance, these pretrained LLMs can also do a broad array of unforeseen tasks when they are given a prompt. This in-context learning capability lets users re-purpose LLMs flexibly for specific tasks with a minimum amount of supervised data, which is very convenient for fast prototyping and experimentation, especially in the low data regime.

But even the largest and most advanced LLMs still have a lot to improve. Grounding and eliminating hallucinations, reasoning and logical clarity, and mathematics are just some examples where LLMs are still behind the best human performance, or in some cases behind the fine-tuned performance of the same model.

The most common way to improve a pretrained model is to fine-tune it on a specialized task or on several tasks. But fine-tuning an LLM usually makes it over-specialized to the fine-tuning tasks, and this harms the generalization ability the model already had on unseen tasks via in-context learning. As we show later, an mT5 model fine-tuned on a single task loses its few-shot performance on unseen tasks within one thousand steps of fine-tuning. When there are hundreds of downstream tasks and even unknown tasks, we want a single fine-tuned model that is good both on the supervised fine-tuned tasks and on general unseen tasks. So it is very important to develop new fine-tuning techniques that prevent these fine-tuned models from over-specializing to only a few tasks.

In this work, we find that the loss of general in-context learning abilities during fine-tuning is to a large extent caused by format specialization, which makes the model overfit to the specific format of the task. For example, if we fine-tune an mT5 model on a binary classification dataset, it learns an output space with only "True" and "False", and it loses its ability to flexibly generate different output styles according to the in-context prompts of other tasks. We show that format specialization tends to happen at the very beginning of fine-tuning, before the model has fully learned the semantic content of the task.

Based on these observations, we propose a simple solution for format specialization: PROmpt Tuning with MOdel Tuning (ProMoT). It off-loads format learning to a small amount of task-specific parameters that are outside the model. ProMoT is a two-stage fine-tuning process. In the first stage, we freeze the pretrained model and tune a small set of additional parameters, and we find that adding a soft prompt before the input is a good choice for this. In the second stage, we freeze the additional parameters and tune the main model. Because the format information is learned first, it mostly goes into the small set of additional parameters. At inference time, we can decide whether to remove the additional parameters or not, depending on whether the incoming task has the same format as the fine-tuned task.

Our experiments show that ProMoT significantly alleviates specialization during fine-tuning, and it also boosts generalization on tasks that are semantically related but have different formats. For example, when an mT5 XXL model is fine-tuned only on an NLI binary classification dataset, it consistently gets better in-context learning performance on summarization than the pretrained model, possibly because of better grounding learned from NLI. Table 1 shows a concrete example. With ProMoT, we can get models that have better supervised performance than pretrained models and also better general in-context learning performance than standard fine-tuning.

To summarize, we have 4 contributions:

- We show empirically that general in-context learning capabilities go down during single-task fine-tuning for T5 models. We identify format specialization as one of the important causes, and it mostly happens at the beginning of fine-tuning.

- We propose a new 2-stage fine-tuning framework, PROmpt Tuning with MOdel Tuning (ProMoT), to reduce format specialization during fine-tuning.

- Experiments on 10+ NLP tasks show that ProMoT significantly reduces the specialization of fine-tuned models compared to standard fine-tuning, while getting similar supervised performance. Less specialization also opens up opportunities to improve generalization across very dissimilar tasks if they share some semantic aspects.

- ProMoT can be combined with many existing fine-tuning and parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods. We show examples where ProMoT is combined with multi-task fine-tuning and with fine-tuning with 1-shot prompts to further improve generalization on unseen tasks.

The most common practice to improve a pretrained model is to fine-tune it on a specialized task or several tasks. As we show later, an mT5 model fine-tuned on a single task loses its few-shot performance on unseen tasks within one thousand steps of fine-tuning. For example, an mT5 [12] model fine-tuned on a binary classification dataset learns an output space with only "True" and "False", losing its ability to flexibly generate different output styles according to the in-context prompts of other tasks.
